#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.
"""

24:- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper with its technical report, the team's last word and work, kept in `Papers/` with their other papers (F-166; F-300). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
34:- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
7:- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work. The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
88:- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

content.content:
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, whether the team made it in a text or in code that it wrote as the language's rule.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. What they learned about the JVM changes the language only where they made it the language's rule. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where a later decision conflicts with the specification's early text, the specification is revised to follow it (P-95 records each change with its reason), and where it conflicts with the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library, the one library follows it. Code is a decision where the team wrote it on purpose, built alike across its types or stated in a commit message, a comment or a checker rule; a stub by its author's words, or a way around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, is not. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The type group's later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings from 2009 and kept so until 2012 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper with its technical report, the team's last word and work, kept in `Papers/` with their other papers (F-166; F-300). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later word contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow it; P-26 says what counts as that word, and when the team's work in the compiler counts. The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
